items.title: Quicksort is usually fast but has a worst case
items.claim: Quicksort and Mergesort are both O(n log n) on average. Where do they differ?

options.text: Quicksort is O(n^2) in worst case (e.g. already-sorted input with naive pivot choice) but in-place and cache-friendly. Mergesort guarantees O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra memory
Quicksort needs more memory than Mergesort

items.reveal:
Tony Hoare invented Quicksort in 1959 while at Moscow State University. With random or median-of-three pivot, the expected runtime is O(n log n) and the in-place property makes it the standard library sort in C (qsort), Java (for primitives) and many others.

Introsort (Musser, 1997) mitigates the worst case by falling back to Heapsort when recursion depth exceeds a threshold. Timsort (Python 2002, Java 2009) is a hybrid Mergesort optimised for partially-sorted real-world data.
items.why: Algorithm choice depends on inputs and constraints. Worst case matters for adversarial inputs (security); average case for benign ones.

items.title: A BST can degenerate into a linked list
items.claim: Inserting elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into a naive binary search tree produces what?

options.text: A balanced tree with O(log n) operations
A 'right-leaning' tree that's effectively a linked list — search becomes O(n), defeating the purpose of a tree

items.reveal:
Self-balancing trees fix this: AVL trees (Adelson-Velsky & Landis, 1962), red-black trees (Bayer 1972, Guibas & Sedgewick 1978), B-trees (Bayer & McCreight 1972).

C++ std::map and Java TreeMap use red-black trees. Linux's process scheduler uses a red-black tree. Databases use B+ trees for indexes because they minimise disk I/O — a different optimisation criterion than in-memory balanced trees.
items.why: Naive implementations of textbook structures can hit worst-case behaviour easily. Production libraries use balanced variants for guaranteed bounds.

items.title: SSDs are dramatically faster but wear out
items.claim: SSDs (NAND flash) and HDDs (spinning disks) have different physical characteristics. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: SSDs are typically 50-100x faster than HDDs for random access, but NAND cells have finite write cycles (typically 1,000-100,000 per cell depending on technology). Wear-levelling firmware spreads writes to extend life
HDDs are always faster than SSDs

items.reveal_title: Speed at the cost of endurance
items.reveal:
HDD random access: ~5-10ms (seek + rotation). SSD random access: ~0.1ms. Sequential bandwidth: ~150MB/s HDD vs 500MB/s (SATA SSD) to 7,000MB/s+ (NVMe).

SLC NAND: ~100,000 write cycles per cell. TLC: ~3,000. QLC: ~1,000. SSD controllers use wear-levelling, over-provisioning and error correction to mask this; consumer SSDs typically last 5-10 years in normal use. HDDs fail mechanically (head crash, motor failure) rather than wearing out by writes.
items.why: Storage choice involves trade-offs of speed, capacity, cost, endurance and physical resilience. The 'right' answer depends on workload.
